The Brief Two locally acquired cases of dengue fever have been confirmed in Hillsborough County, prompting mosquito control officials to step up surveillance and treatment efforts. Unlike most dengue cases seen locally, officials say neither patient recently traveled, suggesting the virus was spread by mosquitoes within Hillsborough County. Mosquito Management Services plans ground inspections, mosquito trapping and targeted treatments in East Tampa and near Picnic Island while urging residents to eliminate standing water and protect themselves from mosquito bites. TAMPA, Fla. - Two confirmed cases of locally acquired dengue fever in Hillsborough County have mosquito control officials taking action to prevent the virus from spreading further. Advertisement Advertisement County crews are preparing to treat areas of potential concern in East Tampa and near Picnic Island in South Tampa after determining both patients likely contracted the virus from mosquitoes within Hillsborough County. Officials say locally transmitted dengue is uncommon and requires an aggressive response. Hillsborough Dengue cases confirmed What we know One of the patients, who asked not to be identified, told FOX 13 he endured about two weeks of severe flu-like symptoms and spent four days in the hospital recovering from the illness. Unlike the travel-related dengue cases Hillsborough County typically sees each year, officials believe neither patient recently visited an area where dengue is common. Instead, investigators say both infections appear to have been acquired locally through mosquito bites. Advertisement Advertisement Because the cases occurred close together geographically, Mosquito Management Services says there could be one or more infected mosquitoes in the area capable of spreading the virus. Inspectors will be going door to door in affected neighborhoods to educate residents, while crews continue setting mosquito traps, collecting thousands of mosquitoes and testing them for viruses such as dengue. Local health officials respond What they're saying Mosquito Management Services spokesperson Gabby Henderson said most dengue cases identified in Hillsborough County are linked to international travel. "Typically, we see a couple cases a year that are travel-related, meaning somebody was in another country, and they came here and developed symptoms that got tested. Because these people have not traveled to any areas they've been staying within our county, that means they got bit by a mosquito that was carrying dengue in Hillsborough County. And because they are close together, that shows us that there may be a mosquito or multiple mosquitoes in that area that are able to spread this virus." Aerial mosquito treatment plans What's next This year also marks the first time Hillsborough County will be able to use its own helicopters to treat adult mosquitoes, rather than relying on outside contractors for aerial adult mosquito control. Advertisement Advertisement Officials say that added capability should allow crews to respond more quickly when mosquito-borne disease concerns arise. Residents are encouraged to eliminate standing water around their homes, wear long sleeves when possible and use mosquito repellent containing DEET to reduce their risk of being bitten. Officials also remind residents that even a bottle cap full of standing water can provide enough space for mosquitoes to breed. The Source The information in this story was gathered from FOX 13 News interviews with Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services, as well as an anonymous dengue fever patient. news.content_title: Second Locally Acquired Dengue Case Confirmed In Hillsborough County
news.content: HILLSBOROUGH COUNTY, Fla. – Health officials in Hillsborough County have confirmed a second case of locally acquired dengue fever. The Florida Department of Health in Hillsborough County (DOH-Hillsborough) announced the diagnosis and stated that local health authorities are working alongside Hillsborough County Mosquito Management to coordinate surveillance and treatment efforts across the area. Dengue is a mosquito-borne virus that typically presents as a flu-like illness. Common symptoms include high fever, severe muscle aches, joint pain, and occasionally a rash, though it generally does not cause respiratory issues. According to health officials, symptoms usually appear within 15 days of a bite from an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. The virus cannot spread directly from person to person. In response to the confirmed case, local health officials are urging residents to take preventative steps to reduce the risk of mosquito bites. Recommended actions include wearing loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and pants, and applying EPA-registered insect repellents to exposed skin and clothing. DOH-Hillsborough noted that these repellents are proven safe and effective when used as directed, including for pregnant and breastfeeding women. Authorities are also asking residents to inspect their homes and yards to eliminate potential breeding sites. Suggestions include repairing broken window or door screens and regularly draining standing water from containers such as buckets, flowerpots, pool covers, garbage cans, and toys. DOH-Hillsborough maintains statewide surveillance for several mosquito-borne illnesses, including West Nile virus, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, malaria, chikungunya, and dengue. Residents who notice dead birds are encouraged to report them to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, as bird mortality can serve as an early indicator of virus activity in the area. Members of the public seeking further details can access the department’s mosquito prevention webpage or review weekly surveillance reports online. Anyone experiencing potential dengue symptoms is advised to contact DOH-Hillsborough directly at 813-307-8010. studies 3 August 2026, 00:01 AM In Focus DENGUE OUTBREAK DENV-3 now dominant strain Say experts; hospitals report rising admissions 4 August 2026, 00:00 AM BANGLADESH SHARE Helemul Alam Helemul Alam Unable to find a seat, a woman sits on the floor with her child at Mugda Medical College Hospital in Dhaka. The child has had a fever for four days, and doctors suspect dengue while awaiting test results. According to the DGHS, at least three people died and 580 others were hospitalised with dengue in the 24 hours until 8:00am yesterday, taking this year’s death toll to 59 and total cases to 16,684. PHOTO: MEHEDI HASAN The DENV-3 serotype has become the dominant strain of the dengue virus in Bangladesh this year, replacing DENV-2, which was the most prevalent last year, according to the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR). A recent IEDCR survey of 71 dengue-positive patients found that 65 (91.55 percent) were infected with DENV-3, while the remaining six (9.23 percent) had DENV-2. Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source By comparison, last year’s surveillance found DENV-2 in 49.2 percent of samples, followed by DENV-3 (35.8 percent), DENV-1 (8.8 percent), and DENV-4 (6.3 percent), IEDCR Director Dr Quazi Ahmed Zaki told The Daily Star. According to dengue experts, the virus has four serotypes -- DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4 -- each comprising several genotypes. Although DENV-2 has historically been linked to major outbreaks, disease severity depends on multiple factors rather than the serotype alone. Zaki cautioned against describing any serotype as inherently more dangerous. “It would not be scientifically accurate to label one dengue serotype as more severe on its own. Disease severity depends on factors including the viral strain, the patient’s immune response, and underlying illnesses,” he said. Zaki said the distribution of serotypes also varies across the country. “Samples from Dhaka and other urban healthcare facilities are different from those collected in the hill tracts and other rural areas,” he said. Image “The overall picture is mixed. Urban areas may show a higher concentration of one serotype, but you cannot generalise the findings for the entire country,” he said. The IEDCR director said previous dengue infection remains one of the strongest risk factors for severe disease. “People who have had dengue before face a higher risk of severe complications, including dengue shock syndrome, if they are infected again,” he said. Patients with kidney disease, liver disease, cancer, or other active infections are also at greater risk of severe illness, regardless of the infecting serotype or whether it is their first dengue infection, he added. He urged public awareness campaigns to focus on repeat infections and underlying health conditions rather than portraying one serotype as universally more dangerous. According to the Directorate General of Health Services, 59 people had died from dengue and 16,684 had been hospitalised this year as of August 3. Meanwhile, physicians say dengue admissions have increased sharply over the past two weeks. HM Nazmul Ahsan, associate professor at Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital, said the hospital has opened two dedicated dengue wards -- one for male and the other for female patients -- after admissions rose to 15-20 patients in each admission cycle. Referring to the latest survey, he said both DENV-2 and DENV-3 are circulating this season, although DENV-3 appears to be more common. Among the four serotypes, DENV-2 and DENV-3 are more severe, Nazmul said. However, the risk of death is higher if a person who previously had dengue is infected with a different serotype, he added. He said many patients are going into shock rapidly, but clinicians have become more experienced in managing severe dengue. For all latest news, follow The Daily Star's Google News channel. “We are seeing patients who deteriorate quite quickly. However, management has improved, and most patients are receiving timely treatment,” he said. Doctors are also reporting a rise in dengue patients with hepatitis this year. “We are seeing considerably more dengue patients with hepatitis than in previous years. Some patients are also dealing with cardiac complications,” he said. He explained that dengue-associated hepatitis requires more than routine fluid management. “When dengue causes hepatitis and liver enzyme levels become markedly elevated, treatment has to be adjusted. These patients require closer monitoring and additional medications beyond standard dengue management,” he said. Ahsan urged people with persistent fever or warning signs to seek medical care promptly, saying early diagnosis and timely treatment remain the best way to prevent severe complications and deaths. news.content_title: Indonesia dengue vaccine prototype revives mRNA misinformation
news.content: Experts say messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines do not alter DNA, contrary to social media posts that resurfaced the long-debunked Covid-era conspiracy theory after Indonesian researchers developed a dengue shot prototype. The new jab is also not controlled by artificial intelligence, as the online rumours allege; the Indonesian Health Ministry told AFP that while AI will be used to predict future virus mutations, it is not a component of the vaccine itself. "Indonesia launches dengue vaccine prototype based on mRNA technology which will be controlled by AI and will alter DNA given from God, breaking the spirituality signal to God," reads part of an Indonesian-language Instagram post shared on July 14, 2026. "The purpose of the vaccine is population shrinking". The post, which has been viewed more than 16,000 times, shares footage of anti-vaccine comments from former health minister Siti Fadilah Supari and local politician Dharma Pongrekun, whom AFP has previously fact-checked for spreading misinformation about hantavirus . "Health has become a very convenient tool to accuse and control nations around the world," Supari says in one of the clips. "For example, we have all experienced what is called Covid. How could people all over the world be deceived about Covid? How could the entire world be vaccinated without knowing what was being put into their bodies?" The post caption goes on to echo another conspiracy theory, previously debunked by AFP , about Indonesia's plan to release mosquitoes infected with the Wolbachia bacteria to help prevent the spread of viruses such as dengue. Screenshot of the false post captured on July 28, 2026, with a red X added by AFP Similar claims have also circulated on Facebook . The University of Indonesia, along with Tsinghua University, successfully developed an mRNA-based dengue vaccine prototype on July 8, saying it has the potential to become the first such jab to reach preclinical trials ( archived link ). Data from the Health Ministry show Indonesia records around 151,000 dengue cases every year -- making it among the country's top diseases with high burden or impacts, alongside tuberculosis, HIV and malaria ( archived link ). Dengue, which spreads through bites from infected mosquitoes and causes severe flu-like symptoms, has exploded globally , fuelled by rising temperatures and densely populated cities ( archived link ). According to the World Health Organization (WHO), nearly half the world's population is at risk, with an estimated 100 million to 400 million infections each year. Factfile on the mosquito-borne dengue virus AFP While dengue vaccines already exist, mRNA shots allow production to be scaled up more quickly since a virus need not be grown in a lab -- and they are generally safer than traditional jabs because they do not contain live pathogens ( archived link ). However, mRNA has become a regular target of conspiracy theories since the Covid-19 pandemic, fuelling baseless claims that such shots cause cancer or alter recipients' DNA . The latest from Indonesia are similarly false. "mRNA vaccines do not alter human DNA and are not controlled by AI," a Health Ministry spokesperson told AFP on July 27. "The mRNA components only carry temporary instructions to form an immune response and then naturally break down". How mRNA works Two live-attenuated vaccines are approved for dengue in Indonesia: Qdenga and Dengvaxia ( archived link ). The former is recommended for patients aged 6-16 in high transmission areas who have not been previously infected with the virus, according to the WHO . The latter jab is being phased out of production (archived links here and here ). Unlike those vacci nes, which contain weakened viruses to train the body's immune response, mRNA shots contain genetic materials that instruct human cells to create proteins matching those of the target pathogen ( archived link ). Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna used the technology in their Covid-19 vaccines developed during the pandemic. How the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine uses genetic information from SARS-CoV-2 to stimulate the body's immune response John SAEKILaurence CHUAFP Thomas Preiss , a professor at Australia's John Curtin School of Medical Research, said that, contrary to the claims swirling online, mRNA vaccines do not "last very long in the body" ( archived link ). "When injected into a person, the mRNA gets into cells mainly around the injection site, and these cells make a tiny amount of a protein that looks like a part of the pathogen you want to achieve protection against," he told AFP in a July 28 email. "The body's immune system detects this and produces a lasting immune response, just like with other vaccines. So while the mRNA vaccine is long gone, the immune system's cells will 'remember' how to respond should a real pathogen enter the body". Manufacturers are developing mRNA vaccines to protect against other diseases, including influenza and HIV ( archived link ). 'No plausible rationale' Preiss said there is "n o plausible rationale nor credible scientific evidence" that Indonesia's mRNA vaccine prototype can "alter the DNA of cells" -- a view shared by other experts contacted by AFP. Lukas Gerstweiler , a senior lecturer at the School of Chemical Engineering at Adelaide University, said the mRNA does not contain the specialised enzymes required to copy RNA into DNA and insert it into a chromosome ( archived link ). "Therefore, an mRNA vaccine cannot alter a person's DNA in the manner claimed in the social media post," he told AFP on July 27. A researcher dilutes messenger RNA (mRNA) at the Inserm ART-RNAm laboratory of the CHR (Regional Hospital Centre) in Orleans, central France on November 18, 2025 JEAN-FRANCOIS MONIERAFP More Mitch Ganley , a research officer at the Department of Microbiology and Immunology at the University of Melbourne, added that mRNA is a common molecule that is "found in almost every cell in the body and is essential for the body to function" ( archived link ). "mRNA vaccines are no more likely to alter the DNA of the individual receiving the vaccine than their own RNA that is much more ubiquitous and abundant," he said on July 27. The Indonesian Health Ministry told AFP that the vaccine is still in the development stage, and "it must undergo a series of preclinical research stages, clinical trials and very strict evaluations" supervised by public health authorities before it is made available to the public. AFP has for years debunked claims that mRNA vaccines alter one's DNA. AI modelling for mutations Gerstweiler of Adelaide University also said AI cannot control an mRNA vaccine, as it consists only of biological molecules -- normally m RNA, lipids and other ingredients ( archived link ). "It does not contain a computer processor, software, communications equipment, sensors or an energy source. It cannot receive commands, monitor a person or make decisions inside the body," he said. "Describing a vaccine as being 'controlled by AI' confuses the use of AI during its design with the physical properties of the finished vaccine". The Indonesian Health Ministry confirmed AI is not a component of the dengue vaccine prototype. "The use of AI in dengue vaccines is to predict possible changes or potential mutations of the virus in the future," a spokesperson said. "The hope is that, through AI modelling, this dengue vaccine will not only be effective against the strains currently circulating, but will also have the potential to provide protection against dengue strains that may emerge in the future"

news.content_original: Experts say messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines do not alter DNA, contrary to social media posts that resurfaced the long-debunked Covid-era conspiracy theory after Indonesian researchers developed a dengue shot prototype. "Indonesia launches dengue vaccine prototype based on mRNA technology which will be controlled by AI and will alter DNA given from God, breaking the spirituality signal to God," reads part of an Indonesian-language Instagram post shared on July 14, 2026. Virginia resident has state’s 1st locally acquired case of dengue fever Catherine Chen | catherine.chen@wtop.com August 5, 2026, 5:43 AM Share This: share on facebook share on X share on threads share on linkedin share on email print The Virginia Department of Health said the patient was sickened by the mosquito-borne virus but had not recently traveled outside the state. Virginia health officials have confirmed the state’s first known case of locally acquired dengue, a viral disease usually associated with international travel. The Virginia Department of Health said the person, who lives in Northern Virginia, became sick but had not recently traveled outside the state. Instead, the patient had been near another Virginia resident who was infected with dengue overseas. Health officials believe a local mosquito likely bit the traveler and later spread the virus to the second resident. Other health news DC region must prepare for disease-carrying mosquitos entering ‘prime-time season’ School backpack overload: Heavy bags can strain kids’ bodies Michigan reports the first 2 US deaths related to a diarrhea-causing parasite Officials said the risk to the public remains low, but the case is a reminder to protect yourself from mosquito bites during the summer months. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, dengue is spread by Aedes mosquitoes and is not passed directly from person to person. Symptoms can include fever, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea and rash. Most people recover within a week, though some infections can become severe and require hospitalization. Health officials recommend using EPA-registered insect repellent and emptying standing water around homes where mosquitoes can breed. According to the Virginia Department of Health, the state’s mosquito season typically runs from early May through early November. Spanberger announces data centers required to pay for new transmission infrastructure Close Local News VDH investigating dengue virus in Northern Virginia, first-ever documented case of virus being acquired locally 10 News Digital Team Published: August 4, 2026 at 2:47 PM Tags: Virginia, Health, Northern Virginia, Virus, Infection, Dengue, Dengue Virus An Aedes aegypti mosquito is pictured at a laboratory of the Center for Parasitological and Vector Studies (CEPAVE) of the national scientific research institute CONICET, in La Plata, Buenos Aires Province, Argentina, on March 26, 2024. Researchers at CONICET are studying the biology, genetic characteristics and behaviour of the Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, transmitter of dengue, zika and chikungunya, and creating biological control strategies as Argentina is facing a significant growing number of dengue cases. (Photo by Luis ROBAYO / AFP) (Photo by LUIS ROBAYO/AFP via Getty Images) (LUIS ROBAYO, AFP or licensors) The Virginia Department of Health announced they are investigating a confirmed case of dengue virus that occurred in a resident in Northern Virginia. The VDH stated that they, along with the Fairfax County and Loudoun County Health Departments, are investigating a case of dengue virus reported in a resident who did not have known travel outside of Virginia before the illness’s onset. This is the first-ever documented case of locally acquired dengue in the commonwealth. Recommended Videos Authorities said the patient was “in close proximity to a recent internationally acquired case in a Virginian who was diagnosed” recently. The dengue virus is spread to people by infected Aedes species mosquitoes. Health officials believe the transmission occurred when a local mosquito bit the resident who was infected with the internationally acquired case of the virus, which then went on to bite the local resident, resulting in the infection. The VDH believes the potential risk for acquiring the virus in the commonwealth remains low, and they are working to monitor for any additional cases. While some cases of dengue can be asymptomatic or have mild symptoms, around one in 20 people develop severe dengue, which is a medical emergency. The following are symptoms of severe dengue: Severe abdominal pain or tenderness Persistent vomiting (≥3 episodes in 1 hr. or ≥4 episodes in 6 hrs.) Clinical fluid accumulation (e.g., pleural effusion, ascites, or pericardial effusion) Mucosal bleeding Altered mental status Liver enlargement Progressive increase of the hematocrit (in at least 2 consecutive measurements taken 6 hours apart). If you are a healthcare provider, health officials recommend the following: Advise patients on strategies to prevent mosquito bites. This will not only reduce risk of dengue but also of mosquito-borne disease endemic to Virginia, such as West Nile Virus. Aedes mosquitoes, which can transmit dengue virus, breed in water-filled containers that may be as small as a bottle cap. Advise patients to “tip and toss” containers around their homes and businesses that may hold water. Obtain a travel history for all patients presenting with acute febrile illness. Consider dengue in patients presenting with fever who live in or recently traveled to areas with risk of dengue. Consider dengue in patients without travel history if presenting with an acute febrile illness and strongly suggestive symptoms, including eye pain, muscle pain, joint pain, and bone pain. Alert your local health department immediately if you suspect dengue illness in a patient who has no history of travel to areas with risk of dengue or other risk factors for dengue infection, such as receiving a blood or organ transplant. Obtain diagnostic testing in suspect cases of dengue virus infection. Review the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidance on dengue case management, including recommendations by patient groups. You can read more information from the VDH here. Smartraveller has urged people heading to the Polynesian island to follow standard safety precautions and use insect repellent. The tropics-associated illness is carried by certain species of mosquito. iStock Advertisement Safe Travel New Zealand found that from January 1 to June 11, the nation had more than 3500 confirmed Dengue cases with more than 150 hospitalisations and three deaths. The tropics-associated illness is carried by certain species of mosquito. Dengue fever is mostly imported into Australia by travellers – if a mosquito bites an infected person, that mosquito can become a carrier. Outbreaks in Australia are largely confined to North Queensland. Advertisement Samoa reportedly had more than 3500 confirmed Dengue cases with more than 150 hospitalisations and three deaths. Supplied Occasionally, dengue fever has proven fatal. Severe dengue fever symptoms may develop several days after the initial symptoms and include frequent vomiting, vomiting with blood in it, and unexpected bleeding. People who have any dengue fever symptoms and are concerned for their health should contact their doctor. Advertisement Advertisement Anybody feeling extremely unwell should contact Triple Zero in Australia or emergency health services overseas. Most cases of the virus have been reported in a few locations including New Caledonia, the Cook Islands and Samoa. Dengue fever presents as a flu-like illness with symptoms that can include high fever, severe muscle and joint pain, intense headaches and skin rash in some cases. Symptoms typically appear within 14 days of being bitten by an infected mosquito. While rarely fatal, the illness can be severely uncomfortable and requires supportive medical care as there is no specific cure. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE Health officials urge residents to eliminate standing water around homes including flower pots, gutters, bird baths, and discarded tires. They also recommend using EPA-approved mosquito repellents, wearing long sleeves and pants when possible, installing or repairing window and door screens, and using air conditioning when available. Palm Beach County Mosquito Control is coordinating with health officials on surveillance and prevention efforts in the affected area. The Department of Health continues statewide monitoring for mosquito-borne illnesses including West Nile virus, Eastern equine encephalitis, and chikungunya. Anyone who develops symptoms should contact their local health department or healthcare provider. For more information on mosquito-borne illness prevention, visit the Florida Department of Health website. news.content: CONTINUE TO SITE CONTINUE TO SITE My account Logout Login News Insurance News Industry News Columns Diversity & Inclusion Mergers & Acquisitions Reinsurance TV Transformation Risk Management Resources Annual Guides Business Strategy E-mag Editorial Panels Events Guides IB Talk Insurance Companies Opinion Premium Content Webinars White papers Best In Insurance Specialty Benefits Catastrophe & Flood Claims Construction & Engineering Cyber Environmental Hospitality Legal Insights Life & Health Marine Motor & Fleet Non-Profits & Charities Professionals Risks Property SME Transformation Travel Workers Compensation IBmarkets Underwriters and Insurers Specialisation Contact Us Contact Us E-newsletter Authors Regular Contributors Advertise IBmarkets - Contact Us Australia United States Canada United Kingdom Australia New Zealand Asia Login Dashboard Travel Samoa dengue: the coverage question brokers cannot leave to claims time Samoa dengue: the coverage question brokers cannot leave to claims time An active Ministry of Health outbreak declaration and an insurer epidemic exclusion are not the same problem – and both apply Travel By Roxanne Libatique Aug 05, 2026 Share A dengue fever outbreak in Samoa – formally declared by the Samoan Ministry of Health in April 2025 and acknowledged in a health sub-advisory by the Australian government – creates two separate coverage problems for travel insurance policyholders. Brokers placing Pacific travel need to understand both before a client travels, because neither issue resolves itself at claims time. Two exclusions, not one Samoa retains a Level 1 “Exercise normal safety precautions” designation on Smartraveller. That matters because it means the destination advisory exclusion – which applies when a “Reconsider your need to travel” or “Do not travel” alert is in place – does not automatically void a policy. What it does not mean is that a dengue claim is straightforwardly covered. The first exposure comes from epidemic and pandemic exclusions. Allianz Australia’s current travel insurance product terms, published on its website, state that its Comprehensive Travel Insurance “has a general exclusion, with limited exceptions, against epidemics and pandemics. That means we don’t cover claims that arise from, or are related to, an epidemic or pandemic.” Samoa’s Ministry of Health has declared a dengue outbreak. Whether an individual insurer classifies that outbreak as an “epidemic” for the purposes of this exclusion is a question brokers must put directly to each insurer – the answer will vary by PDS. The second exposure is the known-event exclusion. Allianz Australia’s product terms state that “there is no cover under any benefit of this policy if your claim arises because you didn’t follow advice or a warning that has been issued by the Australian government or a reliable mass media source.” Smartraveller’s advisory for Samoa, last updated August 5, 2026, explicitly states that Samoa’s Ministry of Health has declared a dengue outbreak and that healthcare systems are facing pressures with the increasing number of cases. That advisory has been live, in updated form, since at least April 2025. The Insurance Council of Australia (ICA) confirms the industry position: most travel insurance policies have exclusions for outbreaks of infectious diseases, pandemics, epidemics, and/or known events. Read next: Known-event exclusions activate across expanded Middle East warning zone Scale of the outbreak From January 1 through June 11, 2026, more than 3,500 confirmed dengue cases, 156 hospitalisations, and three deaths were reported across the Pacific region. Six Pacific island countries and territories – American Samoa, Kiribati, New Caledonia, Samoa, Tonga, and Tuvalu – were reporting active outbreaks as of June 11, with New Caledonia recording the highest case numbers in 2026. Why evacuation cover matters more here than elsewhere For any claim that does respond, the financial exposure is high. Smartraveller is explicit: hospital and medical facilities in Samoa are very limited, all foreigners must pay for health services – with cash typically required before treatment – and in the event of a medical emergency, evacuation by air to Australia or New Zealand is likely the only option. There is no helicopter service, blood supplies are often limited, and medical evacuations may be delayed if commercial airlines are used. Smartraveller states that Australians should hold comprehensive travel insurance covering medical evacuations, noting the Australian government will not pay for these costs. Broker obligations are specific Under Australian law, a general insurance broker who is a licensee or authorised representative must provide financial services efficiently, honestly, and fairly. The National Insurance Brokers Association (NIBA) Insurance Brokers Code of Practice requires brokers to act honestly and with integrity and to communicate with clients in a clear and timely manner. Where the insurance market offers different terms that might meet a client’s needs, the broker should take care to explain the range of available cover and the advantages and disadvantages of each, so the client can make an informed choice. Where an active outbreak has been publicly declared at a destination, a broker who places a policy without advising the client that dengue fever may fall within an epidemic exclusion, or within the policy’s known-event provisions, is not meeting that standard. ICA CEO Andrew Hall made the disclosure expectation clear in October 2025: “Understanding your policy and assessing what kinds of activities you plan on undertaking while you’re travelling is the best way to make sure you’re protected. Check Product Disclosure Statements and speak directly to insurers with any questions.” The awareness gap The 2025 ICA and DFAT Travel Insurance Survey, a national survey of 1,001 Australian travellers, found that while around 70% of respondents were aware of Australian government travel advisories, almost half were unaware that travel insurance would likely not cover travel to destinations subject to a Level 4 (“Do not travel”) advisory. Awareness was lower among younger travellers, who were more likely to underestimate the impact of travel advisories on insurance cover. Samoa’s Level 1 status is precisely the condition that creates false comfort. One in seven Australian travellers went overseas without any cover at all, with one in three of those who skipped insurance deciding against it because they considered their destination safe. Read next: Bali theft fears mask travel insurance’s biggest claims risk Exposure scale Australians comprised 24% of all visitors to Samoa in the first half of 2025, making Australia the second-largest source market after New Zealand. For brokers with clients travelling to Samoa now, three actions are non-negotiable: confirm with each insurer how it classifies the Samoa dengue outbreak under its epidemic and known-event exclusions; verify that medical evacuation cover is explicitly included; and document the advice provided to the client. The Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) complaints environment – where general insurance complaints rose 17% to 34,231 in 2024-25, with denial of claim based on exclusion among the leading complaint categories – makes that documentation commercially as well as professionally important. analysis.time: Publication date: August 4, 2026. Event period: Dengue outbreak declared by Samoan Ministry of Health in April 2025, with ongoing cases reported through June 11, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Samoa (Pacific island), with affected population including travelers, particularly Australians who comprised 24% of visitors in the first half of 2025.
analysis.event: Confirmed dengue fever outbreak in Samoa, declared by the Samoan Ministry of Health in April 2025, acknowledged by Australian government health advisories, and classified as a Level 1 'Exercise normal safety precautions' destination on Smartraveller.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Over 3,500 confirmed dengue cases, 156 hospitalizations, and three deaths reported across the Pacific region from January 1 to June 11, 2026, with Samoa among six Pacific territories reporting active outbreaks. Risk includes limited healthcare facilities, high costs for foreigners, and potential need for costly medical evacuations.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Brokers must confirm insurer classifications of the outbreak under epidemic and known-event exclusions, verify medical evacuation coverage, and document client advice. Uncertainty exists regarding how individual insurers classify the outbreak as an 'epidemic,' and awareness gaps among travelers regarding insurance coverage limitations.

analysis.brief_en: Samoa is experiencing a confirmed dengue fever outbreak declared by its Ministry of Health in April 2025, with over 3,500 cases reported across the Pacific region by mid-2026. Despite being classified as Level 1 on Smartraveller, the outbreak creates significant insurance coverage challenges due to epidemic and known-event exclusions in most travel policies. Brokers face obligations to advise clients on these exclusions and ensure medical evacuation coverage, as healthcare facilities in Samoa are limited and costly for foreigners. The outbreak highlights awareness gaps among travelers, with many unaware that even Level 1 advisories can affect insurance coverage. Insurers vary in their classification of the outbreak, necessitating direct confirmation by brokers.
analysis.summary_en: Samoa is experiencing a confirmed dengue fever outbreak declared by its Ministry of Health in April 2025, with over 3,500 cases reported across the Pacific region by mid-2026. Despite being classified as Level 1 on Smartraveller, the outbreak creates significant insurance coverage challenges due to epidemic and known-event exclusions in most travel policies. Brokers face obligations to advise clients on these exclusions and ensure medical evacuation coverage, as healthcare facilities in Samoa are limited and costly for foreigners. The outbreak highlights awareness gaps among travelers, with many unaware that even Level 1 advisories can affect insurance coverage. Insurers vary in their classification of the outbreak, necessitating direct confirmation by brokers.

elements_zh.time: 发布日期:2026年8月4日。事件期间:萨摩亚卫生部于2025年4月宣布登革热暴发,持续报告病例截至2026年6月11日。
elements_zh.location_and_population: 萨摩亚(太平洋岛屿),受影响人口包括游客,特别是澳大利亚人,2025 年上半年游客人数占 24%。
elements_zh.event: 萨摩亚确认 登革热 暴发,由萨摩亚卫生部于 2025 年 4 月宣布,得到澳大利亚政府健康咨询认可,并在 Smartraveller 上被列为 1 级“采取正常安全预防措施”目的地。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 2026 年 1 月 1 日至 6 月 11 日,太平洋地区报告了超过 3,500 例登革热确诊病例、156 例住院治疗和 3 例死亡,其中萨摩亚是报告活跃 暴发 的六个太平洋地区之一。风险包括医疗设施有限、外国人的高昂费用以及可能需要昂贵的医疗后送。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 经纪人必须确认 暴发 在流行病和已知事件排除项下的保险公司分类,核实医疗后送承保范围,并记录客户建议。各个保险公司如何将 暴发 归类为“流行病”以及旅行者对保险承保限制的认识存在差距,存在不确定性。

news.title_zh: 萨摩亚登革热:承保范围问题经纪人不能留出索赔时间
news.source_body_en: Samoa is experiencing a confirmed dengue fever outbreak declared by its Ministry of Health in April 2025, with over 3,500 cases reported across the Pacific region by mid-2026. Despite being classified as Level 1 on Smartraveller, the outbreak creates significant insurance coverage challenges due to epidemic and known-event exclusions in most travel policies. Brokers face obligations to advise clients on these exclusions and ensure medical evacuation coverage, as healthcare facilities in Samoa are limited and costly for foreigners. The outbreak highlights awareness gaps among travelers, with many unaware that even Level 1 advisories can affect insurance coverage. Insurers vary in their classification of the outbreak, necessitating direct confirmation by brokers.
news.content_zh: 萨摩亚卫生部于 2025 年 4 月宣布出现 登革热 暴发 确诊病例,到 2026 年中期,整个太平洋地区报告了 3,500 多例病例。尽管 暴发 在 Smartraveller 上被列为 1 级,但由于大多数旅行保单中的流行病和已知事件除外,暴发 给保险承保带来了巨大的挑战。由于萨摩亚的医疗设施有限且对外国人来说费用昂贵,经纪人有义务就这些排除情况向客户提供建议,并确保医疗后送覆盖范围。暴发 凸显了旅行者之间的认知差距,许多人没有意识到即使是 1 级建议也会影响保险范围。保险公司对 暴发 的分类各不相同,需要经纪人直接确认。

analysis.brief_en: Fairfax County and other Virginia health departments are investigating the state's first documented locally acquired dengue virus infection, announced on August 5, 2026. The patient had no known recent travel outside Virginia but was in close contact with a previously diagnosed internationally acquired case. This marks a significant public health development as local transmission of dengue is rare in the region. Health officials are working to determine the extent of potential exposure and assess any ongoing risk. The investigation involves multiple agencies to ensure comprehensive monitoring and response.

They also mentioned that there usually aren't respiratory symptoms. By Esteban Balta • Published August 3, 2026 • Updated on August 3, 2026 at 1:54 pm Log in or create a free profile to save articles BOOKMARKER Live Mute ShareToggle Fullscreen You’re watching the NBC6 South Florida News streaming channel, which plays local South Florida news 24 hours a day, seven days a week. You can find the “NBC6 South Florida News” streaming channel on your phone or computer, and on Peacock, Samsung, Roku, Xumo or on our app, so you can watch our local news on your schedule. The Florida Department of Health in Miami-Dade (DOH-Miami-Dade) issued a mosquito-borne illness alert on Monday. This alert comes after one confirmed case of dengue fever in the local area, according to the DOH-Miami-Dade. Watch NBC6 free wherever you are WATCH HERE DOH-Miami-Dade said dengue presents itself with flu-like symptoms like fevers, joint and muscle pain, and sometimes a rash. They also mentioned that there usually aren't respiratory symptoms. Dengue symptoms, the DOH-Miami-Dade said, appear within 14 days of being bitten by an Aedes aegypti mosquito. They also said dengue fever is not contagious. The DOH-Miami-Dade recommends people to: Apply bug repellent Treat your clothing and gear with products that have .5% permethrin Empty standing water at least once a week, which includes things like coolers and buckets, as mosquitoes breed in standing water Use an air-conditioner and keep screens on all windows to keep the mosquitoes outside For more information, click here. news.content_title: Dengue case in Miami-Dade triggers a mosquito alert, health officials say
news.content: People across Miami-Dade County should take precautions to avoid mosquito bites following a confirmed locally acquired case of dengue, according to the Florida Department of Health. Symptoms of dengue appear within 14 days of a bite from an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito and can present "as a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain, fever and sometimes a rash," the Florida Department of Health in Miami-Dade said in a Monday statement. There are typically no respiratory symptoms. People should protect themselves with insect repellent, empty anything that could hold water to stop mosquito breeding and keep them outside by using window screens and air conditioning, the statement said. The Florida Department of Health in Miami-Dade and Miami-Dade County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance, prevention and control efforts, the statement said. MORE: The most annoying season has started in Miami — and the mosquitoes are biting So far this year, 21 cases of dengue have been reported in Miami-Dade, according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For more information, visit the department's mosquito prevention webpage or the weekly mosquito-borne illness surveillance reports . Those who are experiencing any symptoms are asked to call the Department of Health in Miami-Dade at 305-324-2400. Most people infected with dengue don't get symptoms, and many recover within a week, according to the Mayo Clinic. But some do get seriously ill and die. People with severe cases of dengue fever can experience severe stomach pain, persistent vomiting, difficulty or rapid breathing, internal bleeding and organ failure, according to the Mayo Clinic. "Symptoms appear 3-14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include sudden onset of fever, severe headache, eye pain, muscle and joint pain," and bleeding, according to the Florida Department of Health. Some people may also experience vomiting and diarrhea. The only way to know if you're sick with dengue is to get tested. The good news is that unlike the flu, dengue is not contagious and can only spread to people by bites from infected mosquitoes. The bad news is that there's no specific treatment for dengue fever. If you do get sick with dengue, the CDC recommends resting as much as possible, staying hydrated and take acetaminophen (Tylenol) to help with fever. Avoid taking "ibuprofen (Advil) or aspirin because they may cause bleeding in more severe cases," as the Miami Herald has previously reported. The best way to reduce your risk of dengue infection is to avoid being bit by the pesky bloodsuckers: ▪ Wear EPA-approved long-sleeve shirts if planning to be outside. And wear pants and socks, too. This may sound blasphemous, especially for those who want to get a tan or were planning to have a "hot girl summer." But if you want to reduce a risk of a bite, leave the shorts, tanks and sandals at home. And make sure to drink lots of water and avoid being out in the sun during the hottest time of the day. You don't want to get heat exhaustion or another heat-related illness. ▪ Use EPA-registered mosquito repellents . The repellents should have DEET, picaridin, oil of lemon eucalyptus, or IR-3535. ▪ Clean out rain gutters. You don't want the gutters clogged with branches and other debris that could make it easier for rain to pool. Check containers, pots, buckets, toys, plastic covers and other items in and around your home to make sure there's no standing water too. Remember, standing water is a mosquito's breeding ground. ▪ Change the water in bird baths, fountains, wading pools and potted plant trays at least once a week, according to the EPA. And if you have a swimming pool, make sure to keep the water treated and circulating. ▪ Replace outdoor lights with yellow "bug lights." These lights are not repellents, but they tend to attract fewer mosquitoes , according to the EPA. Peter Lynch, 61, died at HMP Moorland in South Yorkshire on 19 October last year. news.content_original: People across Miami-Dade County should take precautions to avoid mosquito bites following a confirmed locally acquired case of dengue, according to the Florida Department of Health. Symptoms of dengue appear within 14 days of a bite from an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito and can present "as a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain, fever and sometimes a rash," the Florida Department of Health in Miami-Dade said in a Monday statement. There are typically no respiratory symptoms. People should protect themselves with insect repellent, empty anything that could hold water to stop mosquito breeding and keep them outside by using window screens and air conditioning, the statement said. The Florida Department of Health in Miami-Dade and Miami-Dade County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance, prevention and control efforts, the statement said. MORE: The most annoying season has started in Miami — and the mosquitoes are biting So far this year, 21 cases of dengue have been reported in Miami-Dade, according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For more information, visit the department's mosquito prevention webpage or the weekly mosquito-borne illness surveillance reports . Those who are experiencing any symptoms are asked to call the Department of Health in Miami-Dade at 305-324-2400. Most people infected with dengue don't get symptoms, and many recover within a week, according to the Mayo Clinic. But some do get seriously ill and die. People with severe cases of dengue fever can experience severe stomach pain, persistent vomiting, difficulty or rapid breathing, internal bleeding and organ failure, according to the Mayo Clinic. "Symptoms appear 3-14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include sudden onset of fever, severe headache, eye pain, muscle and joint pain," and bleeding, according to the Florida Department of Health. Some people may also experience vomiting and diarrhea. The only way to know if you're sick with dengue is to get tested. The good news is that unlike the flu, dengue is not contagious and can only spread to people by bites from infected mosquitoes. The bad news is that there's no specific treatment for dengue fever. If you do get sick with dengue, the CDC recommends resting as much as possible, staying hydrated and take acetaminophen (Tylenol) to help with fever. Avoid taking "ibuprofen (Advil) or aspirin because they may cause bleeding in more severe cases," as the Miami Herald has previously reported. The best way to reduce your risk of dengue infection is to avoid being bit by the pesky bloodsuckers: ▪ Wear EPA-approved long-sleeve shirts if planning to be outside. And wear pants and socks, too. This may sound blasphemous, especially for those who want to get a tan or were planning to have a "hot girl summer." But if you want to reduce a risk of a bite, leave the shorts, tanks and sandals at home. And make sure to drink lots of water and avoid being out in the sun during the hottest time of the day. You don't want to get heat exhaustion or another heat-related illness. ▪ Use EPA-registered mosquito repellents . The repellents should have DEET, picaridin, oil of lemon eucalyptus, or IR-3535. ▪ Clean out rain gutters. You don't want the gutters clogged with branches and other debris that could make it easier for rain to pool. Check containers, pots, buckets, toys, plastic covers and other items in and around your home to make sure there's no standing water too. Remember, standing water is a mosquito's breeding ground. ▪ Change the water in bird baths, fountains, wading pools and potted plant trays at least once a week, according to the EPA. And if you have a swimming pool, make sure to keep the water treated and circulating. ▪ Replace outdoor lights with yellow "bug lights." These lights are not repellents, but they tend to attract fewer mosquitoes , according to the EPA. Peter Lynch, 61, died at HMP Moorland in South Yorkshire on 19 October last year. analysis.brief_en: Virginia health officials have confirmed the first locally-transmitted case of dengue fever in Northern Virginia, marking a significant public health development. According to the Virginia Department of Health (VDH), the case likely resulted from a mosquito biting an infected international traveler and subsequently transmitting the virus to a local resident. This represents the first instance of local dengue transmission in the region. Health authorities are urging residents to take precautions against mosquito bites, though no additional cases or specific risk assessments have been disclosed. The confirmation underscores the importance of mosquito control measures and awareness of mosquito-borne illnesses in the area.

Staletovich Published August 3, 2026 at 2:06 PM EDT Threads Facebook Twitter Pinterest Bluesky LinkedIn Email Gaston De Cardenas / MIAMI HERALD FILE - Fran Middlebrooks, a groundskeeper at Pinecrest Gardens, uses a blower to spray for mosquitoes in August 2016 during an outbreak of Zika in South Florida. The Florida Department of Health announced Monday that it had confirmed a locally-transmitted case of dengue fever in Palm Beach as well as Miami-Dade County. The report marks the third local case for the mosquito-borne disease this year. In July, officials confirmed the first local case in Hillsborough County. Another 49 travel-related cases of dengue have been confirmed across Florida as of July 25. READ MORE: Cutting Florida property taxes could take a bite out of mosquito control The news comes as voters prepare to decide on a statewide property tax amendment that would cut funding to services, including the state’s independent mosquito control districts. According to state health records, a case of West Nile virus confirmed in Alachua County in May is the only other local case of a mosquito-borne illness. As of July 25, 39 travel cases of Chikungunya have also been reported in counties across the state. Those include 19 in Miami-Dade, three in Palm Beach, two in Monroe and one in Broward. Other travel-related cases of dengue include 21 in Miami-Dade, six in Broward and four in Palm Beach. Health officials say dengue can presents as a flu-like illness with muscle aches, join pain, fever and sometimes a rash. Symptoms can manifest within 14 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito. This is a News In Brief report. Visit WLRN News for in-depth reporting from South Florida and Florida news. news.content_zh: 佛罗里达州卫生官员已确认迈阿密戴德县和棕榈滩县出现两例本地传播的登革热病例,使今年当地病例总数达到三例。该公告于 2026 年 8 月 3 日发布,此前希尔斯伯勒县 7 月报告了第一例当地病例。截至 7 月 25 日,全州范围内已确认 49 例与旅行相关的登革热病例,还报告了更多基孔肯雅热和西尼罗河病毒病例。登革热是一种由蚊子传播的疾病,会出现类似流感的症状,包括发烧、肌肉酸痛和关节痛,通常在被蚊子叮咬后 14 天内出现。卫生当局敦促保持警惕,因为这些病例与有关可能削减蚊虫控制服务资金的讨论同时发生。

Subscribe Health News Florida Locally acquired cases of mosquito-borne dengue reported in Palm Beach, Miami-Dade WUSF | By Rick Mayer Published August 3, 2026 at 5:21 PM EDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Joe Mario Pederson / Central Florida Public Media Aedes aegypti mosquitos in a case at the Orange County Mosquito Control headquarters in Orlando. The Florida Department of Health offices in both counties said they are working with mosquito control agencies to monitor and respond to the cases. Florida health officials have confirmed locally acquired cases of dengue fever in Palm Beach and Miami-Dade counties, prompting mosquito surveillance and prevention efforts. The state Department of Health offices in both counties said they are working with their respective mosquito control agencies to monitor and respond to the cases. The offices did not provide additional details about the individuals who contracted the virus. Dengue is spread through the bite of an infected female Aedes aegypti mosquito and is not transmitted person-to-person. The mosquito is known for laying eggs that can be dormant for up to eight months until rains come, leading to a population boom. ALSO READ: Google wants to release 32 million invasive mosquitoes in Florida. Here's why Florida recorded 62 locally acquired dengue cases in 2025, with an unusual concentration in Brevard County, which reported 35 cases — more than half of the state total. Miami-Dade reported 25 locally acquired cases last year. ALSO READ: Cutting Florida property taxes could take a bite out of mosquito control Symptoms typically appear within two weeks of a mosquito bite and can include fever, severe muscle and joint pain, and sometimes a rash. The illness often resembles the flu but usually does not cause respiratory symptoms. Patients typically recover within a couple of weeks. ALSO READ: Less buzzing now, but summer rain will bring a Florida mosquito boom Three local dengue cases have now been reported in the state this year, with one in Hillsborough County in July. There were 49 travel-related cases as of July 25, including 21 in Miami-Dade. Officials are urging residents to prevent mosquito bites by using insect repellent, wearing long sleeves and pants when possible, and removing standing water where mosquitoes can breed. The health department said it would continue statewide surveillance for mosquito-borne illnesses, including West Nile virus, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, malaria, chikungunya and dengue. According to the state arbovirus database, a case of West Nile virus in Alachua County in May is the only other local case of a mosquito-borne illness in 2026. There have been 39 travel cases of Chikungunya this year: Miami-Dade (19), Hillsborough (8), Palm Beach (3), two each in Monroe and Orange, and one each in Alachua, Broward, Hernando, Okaloosa and Osceola. Residents are encouraged to report dead birds to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. Dead birds can be evidence that a mosquito virus is active nearby. analysis.brief_en: Japanese pharmaceutical company Takeda is seeking to have its dengue vaccine Qdenga included in India's national immunization program. This follows the recent approval of Qdenga by India's Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, making it the first vaccine ever approved for dengue prevention in the country. The move comes as India reported 120,000 dengue cases last year. Takeda's senior executive confirmed the company's goal to integrate the vaccine into India's shots program, though no timeline for implementation has been disclosed. The approval marks a significant step in combating dengue, a disease that poses a substantial public health challenge in India.

supplementary_news.content_title: India’s dengue burden: All 4 virus strains circulate together in several states, DENV 2 most widespread
supplementary_news.content:
The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) has revealed that four dengue virus serotypes - 1,2,3,4 have been simultaneously circulating across India, a trend that may shape the country’s dengue preparedness strategies.

The study, conducted by the ICMR through its Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratory (VRDL) network, analysed 6,889 laboratory-confirmed dengue samples collected from 45 laboratories across 25 States and Union Territories (UTs) between May 2023 and May 2025. DENV-2 was the most frequently reported serotype nationwide, accounting for 51 per cent of tested cases. It was followed by DENV-3 (13 per cent), DENV-1 (7 per cent) and DENV-4 (1 per cent).

Researchers found that every state and UT included in the study had at least two dengue serotypes circulating, indicating that dengue has become increasingly hyperendemic across India. According to the study, India contributes to 34 per cent (33 million) of the global burden of symptomatic dengue infections. Approximately 8.9 to 12.6 million primary infections are estimated to occur annually in the country among people aged 5 to 45.

.India gets its first Dengue vaccine—QDENGA.

“Molecular surveillance of dengue serotypes at regular intervals is critical for understanding serotype transmission dynamics and their burden on public health,” the authors wrote. They felt that earlier studies, although valuable, “were confined to smaller geographies” and “were not representative of temporal patterns.” Hence, could not be used for planning national strategies.

“The enhanced testing capabilities at the site laboratories also establish a robust platform for responding to future dengue epidemics, which pose a significant healthcare burden due to climate change, spread of vector mosquitoes and rapid urbanisation.”

Another concerning factor was patients facing concurrent infections. The study noted that such people were more likely to face thrombocytopenia (extremely low platelet count), hemorrhagic manifestations, and severe joint issues.

In most cases, dengue infection causes high fever, headache, weakness and muscle pain, but in severe cases it can be life-threatening. It can potentially lead to organ failure or severe bleeding if left untreated for a long time.

(CBS12) — Health officials issued a mosquito-borne illness advisory Monday after confirming a locally acquired case of dengue fever in Palm Beach County. The Florida Department of Health in Palm Beach County said it is working with Palm Beach County Mosquito Control to conduct surveillance and prevention efforts following the confirmed infection. A locally acquired case means the person was infected by a mosquito in the area rather than while traveling to a place where dengue is more common. Health officials did not release information about the patient or identify where in Palm Beach County the infection is believed to have occurred. Dengue is spread to people through the bite of an infected mosquito. The illness can cause fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting and a rash. Some infections can develop into severe dengue, which may cause serious bleeding, shock or other potentially life-threatening complications. Virginia resident has state’s 1st locally acquired case of dengue fever Catherine Chen | catherine.chen@wtop.com August 5, 2026, 5:43 AM Share This: share on facebook share on X share on threads share on linkedin share on email print The Virginia Department of Health said the patient was sickened by the mosquito-borne virus but had not recently traveled outside the state. Virginia health officials have confirmed the state’s first known case of locally acquired dengue, a viral disease usually associated with international travel. The Virginia Department of Health said the person, who lives in Northern Virginia, became sick but had not recently traveled outside the state. Instead, the patient had been near another Virginia resident who was infected with dengue overseas. Health officials believe a local mosquito likely bit the traveler and later spread the virus to the second resident. Other health news DC region must prepare for disease-carrying mosquitos entering ‘prime-time season’ School backpack overload: Heavy bags can strain kids’ bodies Michigan reports the first 2 US deaths related to a diarrhea-causing parasite Officials said the risk to the public remains low, but the case is a reminder to protect yourself from mosquito bites during the summer months. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, dengue is spread by Aedes mosquitoes and is not passed directly from person to person. Symptoms can include fever, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea and rash. Most people recover within a week, though some infections can become severe and require hospitalization. Health officials recommend using EPA-registered insect repellent and emptying standing water around homes where mosquitoes can breed. According to the Virginia Department of Health, the state’s mosquito season typically runs from early May through early November.
